title: No compulsion, again
hookLine: no compulsion (2:256), would you compel (10:99), to you your way (109:6)

lines: A VOW, AND SONS RAISED JEWISH.
cards: The story starts with a vow. A report in Abu Dawud says that among the Ansar of Medina, the helpers of the Prophet ﷺ, a mother whose babies kept dying would promise: if this child lives, I'll raise him among the Jews.
So some of their sons had grown up Jewish. Then a Jewish tribe, the Banu Nadir, was sent out of the city, and these sons were among them. Their families said: we won't let our sons go.
The report says that's when a verse came down. Four words in Arabic. You may know them by heart.

teach.h: LA IKRAHA: NO FORCING THE HEART.
teach.b: Al-Baqarah, verse two hundred fifty-six, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no compulsion in religion." La ikraha fid-din.
Ikrah comes from k-r-h, the root of disliking something, so compulsion is making someone do what they inwardly refuse. The verse goes on: the right way has become clear from the wrong.
Clear enough to choose, and so it must be chosen. In the report, the sons were left to their choice. Then the two verses beside it.
Surah ten, Yunus, verse ninety-nine: if your Lord had willed, everyone on earth would have believed, all together.
Would you then compel people until they believe? The question answers itself. Allah could have made everyone believe, and didn't; faith is left to be chosen.
Surah eighty-eight is plainer: you are only a reminder; you are not a warden over them. And al-Kafirun, surah one hundred nine, ends: "Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion." Not a shrug.
A boundary drawn with respect, by someone sure of their own way. Over the centuries, scholars debated how far 2:256 reaches.
Some classical scholars limited it, or held that later verses had abrogated it; others read it as a general rule.

teach.h: TO YOU YOURS, TO ME MINE.
teach.b: That debate is part of the tradition. Three angles, then. The truth has been made clear.
Even a prophet doesn't force it. And when people choose differently, each keeps their own way.

how: Muslims often cite 2:256, 10:99 and 109:6 as the Qur'an's teaching that faith cannot be forced; surah al-Kafirun is short and widely recited, including in the sunnah prayers.

o: religion has no rules anyone must follow
nobody needs to pray unless they feel like it
faith can't be forced; it has to be chosen

p: to you yours, to me mine

s: the Qur'an says the Prophet should make people believe
10:99 asks: would you then compel people until they believe?
a report ties 2:256 to sons of the Ansar raised Jewish
in Abu Dawud: they were left to their choice.
ikrah comes from a root about disliking
k-r-h: forcing someone to do what they don't want.

games.q: you're in Medina. sons of your community, raised Jewish, are leaving with a Jewish tribe. families want to hold them back. what does the verse that came down say?
o: there is no compulsion in religion.
games.why: 2:256 came down, the report says, and they were left to their choice.

practice: Bring to mind someone close who chose differently from you: a faith, no faith, a way of living. Notice whatever tightens, and without agreeing, say inside: your way is yours.
If there's something you've been pushing them on, picture setting it down; you can still care, and still hope, without compelling.

wordCard.voice: No compulsion. La ikraha fid-din: the heart can't be forced, even a prophet isn't a warden, and to each their own way. Today's word.
